Зүүнээс scan хийж олж болно. Харин sorted учраас дундах утга $x$-ээс бага байвал түүний зүүн талд хариу байхгүй. Нэг comparison-оор олон элементийг хасаж чадна.
Энэ ганц хичээл half-open зааг хэрэглэнэ: эхлээд $l=0,r=n$. $a[\mathrm{mid}]<x$ бол $l=\mathrm{mid}+1$. Үгүй бол mid хариу байж болох тул $r=\mathrm{mid}$. Зааг тэнцэхэд хайлт дуусна.

Эхний $a[i]\ge x$ index-ийг олохдоо array-ийн утгууд биш, “$a[i]\ge x$ үнэн үү?” гэсэн Boolean дарааллыг хар. Sorted array-д false-уудын дараа true-ууд орно. Binary search энэ шилжилтийн заагийг олно; true элемент огт байхгүй бол зааг $n$.

Loop-ийн invariant: $l$-ээс өмнөх бүх index false, $r$-ээс эхэлсэн хүчинтэй index-үүд true. $[l,r)$ доторх хэсэг хараахан шийдэгдээгүй. $a[mid]<x$ бол mid болон зүүн хэсэг false тул $l=mid+1$. Үгүй бол mid true тул $r=mid$; mid өөрөө хариу байж болохыг хадгална.

$l<r$ үед mid үргэлж хүчинтэй index бөгөөд аль branch-д ч хүрээ багасна. $l=r$ үед шийдээгүй хэсэг хоосон: энэ байрлал false ба true-ийн яг зааг. Lower bound-ийн хариу заавал $x$-тэй тэнцүү утга байх албагүй.

Нэг query-д linear scan хамгийн муудаа $n$ утга шалгана; $q$ query-д $O(nq)$. Харин нэг удаа эрэмбэлээд query бүрд зааг хайвал $O(n\log n+q\log(n+1))$. Оролт аль хэдийн sorted бол sort-ийн зардал хэрэггүй. Ганц query-д эрэмбэлэх нь linear scan-аас илүү ашигтай байх албагүй.

Жишээний index нь sorted array дахь байрлал. Анхны эрэмбэлээгүй array-ийн index хэрэгтэй бол sort хийхэд утга болон original index-ийг хамт хадгал; эрэмбэлсний дараах index-ийг анхны index гэж буцааж болохгүй.

en.title: Binary search — searching a sorted array
en.summary: Halve the search range by safely discarding an irrelevant half.

blocks.text: In $a=[2,4,4,7,9]$, find the first index whose value is at least $x=4$. The answer is $1$, even though $4$ appears twice.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: A left-to-right scan works, but sorted order lets us eliminate many candidates at once: if the middle value is too small, everything to its left is too small too.
This search uses half-open bounds: start with $l=0,r=n$. If $a[\mathrm{mid}]<x$, set $l=\mathrm{mid}+1$. Otherwise mid may still be the answer, so set $r=\mathrm{mid}$. Stop when the boundaries meet.

To find the first $a[i]\ge x$, view the Boolean sequence “is $a[i]\ge x$?”. In a sorted array, false positions precede true positions. Binary search locates this boundary, which is $n$ if no true position exists.

The invariant is that every index before $l$ is false and every valid index from $r$ onward is true. The undecided region is $[l,r)$. If $a[mid]<x$, move $l$ to $mid+1$; otherwise set $r=mid$, preserving mid as a possible boundary.
When $l<r$, mid is a valid index and either branch shrinks the range. At $l=r$, nothing remains undecided, so this is the exact boundary. A lower-bound result need not contain a value equal to $x$.

A linear scan checks up to $n$ values per query, costing $O(nq)$ for $q$ queries. Sorting once and searching each boundary costs $O(n\log n+q\log(n+1))$. Already sorted input needs no sorting; for one query, sorting may be worse than scanning.
The returned index belongs to the sorted array. If an application needs an original unsorted index, retain it alongside the value; sorting changes positions.

sections.title: 7. Why is it correct and how fast is it?

items: Initially $0\le l\le r\le n$. Every index before $l$ has value below $x$, and every valid index at or after $r$ has value at least $x$. Both claims hold vacuously for $l=0,r=n$.

If $a[\mathrm{mid}]<x$, sorted order makes every index $i\le\mathrm{mid}$ false, so moving $l$ to $\mathrm{mid}+1$ loses no answer. Otherwise $a[\mathrm{mid}]\ge x$ and every index to its right qualifies, so setting $r=\mathrm{mid}$ preserves the invariant.

Each iteration decreases $r-l$. At termination $l=r$: every earlier index is false, and if $l<n$, then $a[l]\ge x$. Thus this is the first qualifying index; $l=n$ means none exists. Never read $a[n]$ without checking the returned boundary.
The code names low/high correspond to $l,r$, middle to $\mathrm{mid}$, and values/target to $a,x$ in the proof.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: In a sorted array, checking the middle lets us discard an entire half that cannot contain the required answer. We never check its elements individually.
The search interval shrinks from $n$ to about $n/2,n/4,n/8$. After $k$ steps about $n/2^k$ candidates remain. It therefore takes $O(\log n)$ steps, each with a constant amount of work.
Example: lower bound on $1024$ positions shrinks the range roughly as $1024\to512\to256\to\cdots\to1$. Depending on the boundary case, the code takes about $10$–$11$ iterations.
The search costs $O(\log n)$ when its middle check is $O(1)$. Multiply by the checker cost otherwise, and include sorting if the input is not already sorted.

One search uses $O(1)$ auxiliary state: two bounds and a midpoint. The complete program still stores an $O(n)$ array and reads $n$ values and $q$ queries. Per-query auxiliary space is not the whole program's memory.

en.title: Greedy — making a safe choice at each step
en.summary: Learn greedy through one concrete problem and the reason its choice is safe.

blocks.text: Movies run during $[1,4),[2,3),[3,5),[5,7)$. Choose the most nonoverlapping movies. Taking $[2,3),[3,5),[5,7)$ gives $3$. A movie may start exactly when the previous one ends.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Trying every subset gives $2^n$ possibilities. Choosing the earliest finishing available movie leaves as much room as possible for later choices.
Do not confuse earliest finish with shortest duration or earliest start. This problem specifically needs earliest finish; another greedy problem may need a different rule.
Greedy commits to a local choice without revisiting it. The objective here is the number of films, not total duration or value. Short duration is not the same selection criterion as early finishing.

Choosing the earliest finish leaves the most room for later films. Replace the first film of an optimal schedule with the earliest-finishing one: its finish cannot increase, so later films remain feasible. This exchange proves that an optimum can include the greedy choice.

Last_end stores the finish of the last accepted film. A later film is compatible when its start is no smaller. Half-open intervals $[l,r)$ permit touching endpoints, explaining the non-strict comparison.

A brute-force oracle can sort by finish, enumerate all $2^n$ subsets and check each selected sequence in that order. This takes $O(n2^n)$ time after sorting: useful for small tests, not for $n=200000$.

sections.title: 7. Why is it correct and how fast is it?

items: Let $G$ be an earliest-finishing available film and $O$ the first film in an optimal maximum-cardinality schedule. Then $f(G)\le f(O)$. Every film scheduled after $O$ starts no earlier than $f(O)$, so it also fits after $G$.

Replacing $O$ with $G$ therefore does not reduce the number of films: an optimal schedule beginning with the greedy choice exists. Apply induction to the same problem restricted to films starting at or after the finish of $G$.

The argument assumes equal unit value per film, one viewer, and intervals $[l,r)$ with $l<r$. It does not solve arbitrary weighted profit: for $[0,2)$ worth $1$ and $[0,3)$ worth $100$, earliest finish chooses the lower profit.

blocks.text: Sorting takes $O(n\log n)$ and scanning $O(n)$. The copied input uses $O(n)$ extra space.

The scan invariant is that the selected count is maximum for the processed finish-order prefix, and among schedules with that count the greedy final finish is earliest. This leaves maximum flexibility for the next film. A skipped film must not replace that state.

items: Not every greedy rule works: justify the choice or search for counterexamples.
Use $l\ge\mathrm{last}$ because touching endpoints are allowed.

blocks.text: For the shortest-duration rule, consider $[0,3),[3,6),[2,4)$. The uniquely shortest interval $[2,4)$ overlaps both others, leaving one film; the first two intervals allow two. This refutes a different rule from the earliest-start counterexample.

Equal finishes leave the same next boundary, but the sort comparator must still be strict rather than treating equality as less-than. Test no films, one film, duplicate films, all-overlapping films and touching endpoints separately.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Instead of examining every subset or viewing order, scan films by increasing finish time. The exchange argument justifies one choice without exploring all alternative branches.

Sorting costs $O(n\log n)$. The scan examines each film once and updates last_end only when selecting it, costing $O(n)$. Sorting dominates the total $O(n\log n)$ time; decisions do not restart a search from the beginning.
Example: $20$ films have $2^{20}=1048576$ possible subsets. After sorting, the greedy scan checks just $20$ films without generating those subsets.
Fast decisions do not prove correctness. Without a valid exchange argument, the same greedy rule can be fast and wrong.

The function receives its vector by value, so the input copy occupies $O(n)$ space. Sorting adds a smaller $O(\log n)$ stack; the copy dominates auxiliary storage. Endpoints use signed 64-bit values and the comparator compares directly rather than subtracting.

sections.title: 12. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: Use it for maximum unweighted interval count. With different values, earliest finishing does not ensure maximum total value; weighted interval DP is needed. Correctness depends on the objective.

blocks.text: $n$ шатанд нэг эсвэл хоёр алхмаар өгсөнө. $n=3$ үед $1+1+1$, $1+2$, $2+1$ гэсэн $3$ арга байна. $n$ том бол хэдэн арга вэ?
Сүүлийн алхмыг $1$ эсвэл $2$ гэж салгасан recursion бичиж болно. Гэхдээ жижиг $n$-ийн хариуг дахин дахин асууна. Нэгэнт бодсон жижиг хариуг array-д хадгалъя.
Сүүлийн алхам $1$ бол өмнө нь $i-1$, $2$ бол $i-2$ дээр байсан. Энэ хоёр бүлэг давхцахгүй тул тоонуудыг нэмнэ. $\mathrm{dp}[i]=\mathrm{dp}[i-1]+\mathrm{dp}[i-2]$.

DP-г formula цээжлэхээс биш state-ийн утга бичихээс эхэл. Энд $dp[i]$ нь яг $i$ гишгүүр хүрэх ordered алхмын дарааллын тоо. $1,2$ ба $2,1$ өөр зам. Зөвхөн сүүлийн хэдэн алхмыг мэдэхэд цаашдын боломж бүрэн тодорхой болох state сонгоно.

Сүүлийн алхам $1$ эсвэл $2$. Эхний бүлэг өмнөх $i-1$-д хүрсэн зам бүрт $1$ нэмснээс, хоёр дахь нь $i-2$-д хүрсэн зам бүрт $2$ нэмснээс үүснэ. Бүлгүүд сүүлийн алхмаараа ялгаатай тул давхцахгүй: $dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2]$.

Base case $dp[0]$=$1$ нь “юу ч хийхгүй” ганц зам. Энэ base байснаар эхний алхмууд ч ижил recurrence-ээр гарна. Өсөх $i$ дарааллаар бодвол унших өмнөх state-үүд бэлэн байна. Memoization ижил state-ийг хэрэгтэй үед recursion-аар, tabulation энэ шиг дарааллаар боддог.

Жишээ нь $\operatorname{ways}(5)$ нь $\operatorname{ways}(4)$ ба $\operatorname{ways}(3)$-ыг дуудна; эхнийх нь $\operatorname{ways}(3)$-ыг дахин дуудна. Ижил remaining-size-ийн хариу давтагдаж байгаа нь хадгалах дохио. Memoization үүнийг recursion дээр cache хийнэ; tabulation нь dependency-ийн дарааллаар урьдчилж бөглөнө.

Naive recursion-ийн гүн хамгийн ихдээ $n$, node бүр хамгийн ихдээ хоёр хүүхэдтэй тул $O(2^n)$ хугацаа гэсэн upper bound гарна; энэ нь tight bound гэсэн үг биш. Call stack $O(n)$. DP нь ижил дэд бодлогыг нэг удаа бодох замаар recursion-ийн давталтыг арилгана.

en.title: Introduction to DP — saving smaller answers
en.summary: Learn states, base cases and transitions one at a time through a stair problem.

blocks.text: Climb $n$ stairs using steps of size one or two. For $n=3$, the routes are $1+1+1$, $1+2$, and $2+1$: three ways. What about larger $n$?

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: A recursion can split by the final step, but repeatedly recomputes the same smaller answers. Save those answers in an array.
A final step of one comes from $i-1$; a final step of two comes from $i-2$. These groups do not overlap, so add their counts: $\mathrm{dp}[i]=\mathrm{dp}[i-1]+\mathrm{dp}[i-2]$.

Start DP by defining a state rather than memorizing a formula. Here $dp[i]$ counts ordered step sequences reaching exactly stair $i$. Sequences $1,2$ and $2,1$ are different. A state must contain all information needed for future choices.
The last step is $1$ or $2$. The first group extends paths to $i-1$ by $1$; the second extends paths to $i-2$ by $2$. Their last steps differ, so the groups are disjoint: $dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2]$.

Base case $dp[0]$=$1$ represents the single empty path. It lets early answers follow the same recurrence. Increasing $i$ ensures dependencies are ready. Memoization computes states on demand through recursion; tabulation fills them in a chosen order.

For example, $\operatorname{ways}(5)$ calls $\operatorname{ways}(4)$ and $\operatorname{ways}(3)$, and the former calls $\operatorname{ways}(3)$ again. Repeated remaining-size answers suggest caching. Memoization caches recursive calls; tabulation fills states in dependency order.

The naive recursion has depth at most $n$ and at most two children per node, giving an $O(2^n)$ time upper bound, not a claim of a tight bound. Its call stack is $O(n)$. DP removes repeated subproblem evaluations.

sections.title: 7. Why is it correct and how fast is it?

items: Define $dp[i]$ as the number of step sequences reaching exactly stair $i$. The base $dp[0]=1$ represents one empty sequence. Setting it to zero would incorrectly make every later state zero.

For $i>0$, the last step has size $1$ or $2$. Removing the final step gives a bijection between the first group and sequences reaching $i-1$. For $i\ge2$, the second group similarly corresponds to $i-2$. These groups are disjoint, so $dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2]$; at $i=1$ only the first group exists.

Processing indices in increasing order means every predecessor is already correct. The base case and this induction prove all states correct. Taking the modulus after addition preserves the required remainder; each addend is below $10^9+7$, so their sum is safe in signed 64-bit arithmetic.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Enumerating all stair-climbing paths repeatedly solves the same remaining subproblems. DP stores the number of ways to reach step $i$ and reuses it without recomputation.
There are $n+1$ states, numbered $0$ through $n$. Each state reads at most two previous answers and adds them: $O(1)$ work. Number of states times work per state gives $O(n)$ time.
Example: for $n=10$ there are $89$ paths, but the code does not store those paths. It uses $11$ DP positions and derives the answer from earlier values.
DP is not always linear. If each state scans all earlier states, it can take $O(n^2)$. This count assumes fixed-width or modular arithmetic.

The full array stores $n+1$ modular counts, using $O(n)$ memory. This recurrence reads only the previous two states, so it can be compressed to $O(1)$ space if both old values survive until the new value is computed. Reconsider that choice when other tasks need all states or reconstruction.

sections.title: 12. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: For counting, minimum-cost and maximum-score DP, first define state, transition, base and evaluation order. Minimum DP often needs INF for unreachable states rather than zero. If identical states have different future options, the state definition is incomplete.

blocks.text: First predict these small cases by hand. Then run the program and compare. A mismatch is a reason to inspect the state definition, boundaries and transition, rather than patching the output.

A small objective variation: heights $[10,30,20]$, jumps of one or two positions, and cost equal to the absolute height difference. Minimum-cost states are $[0,20,10]$: the last is $\min(20+10,0+10)=10$. The predecessor positions resemble the counting example, but the combination operation differs.

Test state sufficiency by asking whether two histories with that state have the same future options. If an activity cannot repeat on consecutive days, day alone is insufficient: distinguish the last activity. Cyclic dependencies also do not automatically fit this increasing-index, one-pass template.
